title: Mechanics
lines: Mechanics is the largest physics topic in USAT. Expect short numericals and one-line concept checks: resolve a vector, apply an equation of motion, find a centripetal force, compare kinetic energies or use Bernoulli's equation. Most questions need two or three lines of working once you know the right formula and keep every quantity in SI units.
## Vectors
A scalar has size only (mass, speed, work, energy, power). A vector has size and direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum, torque).
- Components: Aₓ = A cos θ, Aᵧ = A sin θ, where θ is measured from the x-axis.
- Resultant: R = √(Rₓ² + Rᵧ²), direction tan θ = Rᵧ/Rₓ, read in the correct quadrant.
- Two forces A and B at angle θ: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ. R is largest (A + B) at 0° and smallest (A − B) at 180°.
- Dot product A·B = AB cos θ is a scalar (work W = F·d). Cross product |A × B| = AB sin θ is a vector at right angles to both (torque τ = r × F).
## Kinematics
For constant acceleration, use the four equations of motion:
| Equation | Missing quantity
| v = u + at | distance
| s = ut + ½at² | final speed
| v² = u² + 2as | time
| s = ½(u + v)t | acceleration
- On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement.
- A body dropped from rest covers distances in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 in successive equal seconds.
- Projectile launched at speed u and angle θ: time of flight 2u sin θ/g, maximum height u² sin² θ/2g, range u² sin 2θ/g. The range is greatest at 45°, and angles θ and 90° − θ give equal ranges.
> Example 1. A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its greatest height and its time in the air.
> At the top v = 0, so 0 = 20² − 2 × 10 × h, giving h = 400 ÷ 20 = 20 m.
> Time to the top = u/g = 2 s. The fall takes the same time, so the ball is in the air for 4 s.
## Newton's laws and momentum
- First law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a net force acts (inertia).
- Second law: F = ma, or more generally F = Δp/Δt, where momentum p = mv (unit kg m/s = N s).
- Third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
- Impulse = FΔt = change in momentum. A longer stopping time means a smaller force (crumple zones, bending the knees on landing).
- With no external force, total momentum is conserved: in all collisions and explosions, including a gun's recoil.
- Elastic collision: kinetic energy is conserved too. Inelastic: some kinetic energy turns into heat and sound. When bodies stick together, the loss is greatest.
! A ball that hits a wall at v and rebounds at v changes its momentum by 2mv, not zero: the direction reverses.
## Circular motion and gravitation
- Angular speed ω = 2π/T = 2πf, and v = rω.
- Centripetal acceleration v²/r = rω², directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r. It is supplied by a real force: tension, friction, gravity or an electric force.
- Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². At the surface g = GM/R².
- Orbital speed v = √(GM/r), independent of the satellite's mass. Escape speed √(2GM/R) = √(2gR), about 11.2 km/s for the Earth.
- A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours.
- Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and their craft are falling freely together; gravity has not vanished.
> Example 2. A 1,000 kg car takes a level bend of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. What sideways friction force is needed?
> F = mv²/r = 1,000 × 10² ÷ 50 = 2,000 N, directed towards the centre of the bend.
## Work, energy and power
- Work W = Fd cos θ (joule). No work is done when the force is at right angles to the motion, such as the centripetal force.
- Kinetic energy ½mv² = p²/2m. Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.
- Gravitational potential energy near the surface = mgh. Without friction, kinetic plus potential energy stays constant.
- Work-energy principle: net work done on a body = its change in kinetic energy.
- Power P = W/t = Fv (watt). 1 hp = 746 W. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
> Example 3. A pump lifts 500 kg of water through a height of 12 m in one minute. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its useful power.
! Kilowatt-hour sounds like power but measures energy. A 2 kW heater used for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
## Fluids
- Pressure at depth h in a liquid: P = P₀ + ρgh. Gauge pressure is ρgh alone.
- Archimedes: upthrust = weight of fluid displaced. A floating body has the fraction ρ(body)/ρ(fluid) of its volume submerged.
- Continuity for steady flow: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Halving a pipe's diameter quarters its area, so the speed rises four times.
- Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant along a streamline, so faster flow means lower pressure (aeroplane lift, spray guns, a swinging cricket ball).
- Stokes' law: drag on a small sphere F = 6πηrv. Terminal velocity is proportional to r².
> Example 4. Water flows at 1 m/s in a pipe of diameter 4 cm, which narrows to 2 cm. Find the speed in the narrow part.
> Area depends on diameter squared: the area becomes (2/4)² = ¼ of the original, so v = 1 × 4 = 4 m/s.
! The speed at the top of a projectile's path is u cos θ, not zero. Only the vertical part of the velocity is zero there.
! mgh is valid only close to the Earth's surface. For large heights use −GMm/r.
## Quick check
- Two equal forces at 120° to each other: resultant? (equal to either force)
- Speed doubled: centripetal force on the same circle? (four times)
- Does the orbital speed of a satellite depend on its mass? (no)
- Pipe diameter halved: speed of flow? (four times)
- Unit of impulse? (N s, the same as momentum)
